title: Children's understanding of other people's minds

paragraphs.text: It is basic to our everyday human understanding that both we and others have beliefs. We know that we ourselves have beliefs about the world, that our beliefs change, that they might be wrong, and that what we say and what we do are based on our beliefs. We also assume that other people have beliefs; they can tell us those beliefs directly, or we can work out their own beliefs indirectly from the way they behave. Understanding that other people have interpretations of the world is often referred to as having a 'theory of mind'.

Psychologists have designed a number of experiments to ascertain at what age children acquire a theory of mind. In one influential experiment, Wimmer and Perner (1983) used models to act out a story about a little boy called Maxi, who put some chocolate in a blue cupboard. Then Maxi left the room, and while he was out of the room the children saw Maxi's mother transfer the chocolate to a green cupboard. Then the children were asked to predict where Maxi would look for the chocolate when he came back into the room. Four-year-olds usually predicted that he would look in the green cupboard. From an adult point of view, this is a very surprising response, because Maxi could not possibly know that the chocolate had been moved. We can infer from such a result that young children do not understand that Maxi's beliefs about the world are different from how the world really is, and they do not understand that he will act on the basis of his beliefs and not on the actual state of the world.

Wimmer and Perner's task is referred to as the 'false-belief' task, because Maxi's belief that the chocolate is in the blue cupboard is an incorrect belief after the chocolate has been moved. Some researchers questioned whether Wimmer and Perner's story was of an appropriate length, and suggested that the children may have had difficulty with the amount of information they needed to consider in order to fully understand the story. Baron-Cohen (1985) reduced the complexity of the story, with a version called the Sally-Anne task. In this version, children are shown two dolls, Sally (who has a basket) and Anne (who has a box). Sally puts a marble in her basket and then leaves. While she is absent, Anne takes the marble from the basket and puts it in the box. Sally returns, and children are asked 'Where will Sally look for her marble?'. The typical result from this task is that four-year-olds realise that Sally will look in the basket, three-year-olds say that she will look in the box. In other words, with this briefer version of the false-belief task, children of four perform correctly, but three-year-olds seem unable to understand how Sally will act.

Although nearly all children achieve success on false-belief tasks at approximately the same age, there are individual differences in that achievement, with some children succeeding at a slightly younger age than others. Several researchers have found that children with better language skills perform better on false-belief tasks. Thus children who have delayed language abilities may show a delay in their ability to perform false-belief tasks (Jenkins and Astington, 1996). Also, some children with hearing impairments have difficulty (Woolfe, 2002).

Some researchers have pointed out that family background may also account for differences. Lewis (1996) carried out a study with children who lived in extended families in the Greek communities of Crete and Cyprus. Lewis gave the children several false-belief tasks and gathered information about the number of people with whom the children interacted on a daily basis. They found that children who were the most successful on the tasks were the children who interacted most with adults and had more older friends and older siblings. The researchers suggested that those young children who have a greater opportunity to talk and interact with older children and adults will have a better chance of developing their theory of mind skills at an earlier age. On the other hand Brown (1996) and his team investigated the way that children who were nearly four years of age talked with mothers, friends and siblings. They collected and examined samples of conversation, and found that children were more likely to talk about thoughts and beliefs when interacting with their siblings and friends than when they were interacting with their mothers. Brown also found a correlation between children's talk of thoughts and beliefs with their siblings and friends and their performance on false-belief tasks.

Dunn (1999) pointed out that there is a rapid increase in the amount of child-child interaction between two and four years of age, and he also suggested that children may learn more from interacting with each other than with adults. He gave two reasons for this suggestion. First, other children may be more likely than adults to take part in pretend activities. Planning and acting out such activities necessitate children discussing their thoughts and ideas with each other. Second, when adults and a young child communicate, the adult will usually take into account the child's lack of conversational experience, and make allowances for the child when structuring the interaction. However, when children talk to each other they are less likely to make such allowances, and therefore successful communication may be more challenging, and force them into explicit consideration of each other's knowledge and beliefs.
